newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin birthday satire portrays haunted president.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin birthday satire portrays haunted president.

text.p: Lonely and tormented, Boris Yeltsin wrestles with the ghosts of communist leaders haunting his Gorky-9 country home. From a corner, his chief aide serenades him towards death with a sombre Beethoven piano melody.

Russia's NTV independent television marked the president's 66th birthday with a cutting satire comparing Yeltsin's "working convalescence" at Gorky-9 with communist state founder Vladimir Lenin's isolation in the months before his death in 1924. Intrigue abounds and his allies use him only for their own ends.

The satire, using rubber puppets, opens with Yeltsin pointing at an old sepia photograph of Lenin sitting in a wheelchair at his country estate, which was also called Gorky. Beside Lenin, amid the snow, sits the scheming Josef Stalin.
"Listen Anatoly, did he live long here?" Yeltsin asks his aide, Anatoly Chubais, in a weak plaintive voice.
"They don't live very long here," Chubais replies wistfully, still playing his melody.
"What?" asks Yeltsin, clearly alarmed.

"Well, they relax and then they return to the Kremlin to active work," Chubais adds, slyly. Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery and pneumonia, is relieved and sighs at the prospect of active work. "So much to do."

The unfortunate coincidence of names in Yeltsin's residence and the estate where Lenin spent his last days, isolated and at the mercy of those, especially Stalin, who controlled access to him, has not been lost on the Russian press.
Opponents portray Yeltsin as too weak to rule; a man brazenly manipulated by a "regent" Chubais.

Yeltsin, wrapped in a heavy scarf and looking up from a volume of Lenin's works, winces at an image of the bearded Bolshevik leader, beckoning him from his wheelchair beneath a snow-spattered arcade of trees outside.
"Anatoly, do you believe in ghosts?" His voice quivers.
"The ghosts of communism? That's all rubbish."
"I tell you," says Yeltsin, wheezing. "He's here."
"One last question, Anatoly, then I won't bother you any more," says the former communist party politburo member, after a pause. "Why is it called Gorky nine?"
"Count for yourself." The soothing music continues.

Yeltsin counts on his fingers the leaders who have passed through Gorky, from Lenin and Stalin to Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Chernenko. "And then that windbag," says Yeltsin in a reference to his enemy Mikhail Gorbachev. "Eight, and then me."
Suddenly, sinister music is heard as Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin telephones Chubais from his approaching limousine.
"I'm on my way," says Chernomyrdin who, in the real Russia, could be a presidential candidate if Yeltsin yielded power.
"I know," says Chubais, furtively.
"How's himself?"
"He's himself...still."

The programme, "Puppets", was broadcast on Saturday night while the real Yeltsin celebrated his birthday at Gorky-9 with his family, Chubais and Chernomyrdin. His wife Naina said he was recovering well.
Chernomyrdin drove straight to the estate from an economic summit in Switzerland bearing a gift he declined to identify. His daughter said she had given Yeltsin a quilted jacket.
"Puppets" ends with Chernomyrdin briefing Yeltsin on developments outside, in Russia. "Everyone is happy. They are celebrating your birthday...Things are moving."
"Moving where?"
"Don't worry. It's bad for you."
"Don't hide the truth from me."
Suddenly Chernomyrdin turns into Stalin before Yeltsin's eyes and begins talking in his characteristic Georgian accent.
"Don't worry," Stalin says, in words he would have used with Lenin. "Just sit here in deepest Gorky and get better, if you can."
With a start, Yeltsin regains his hold on reality and Stalin again gives way to the portly figure of Chernomyrdin "What was that?" the president asks.
"It was nothing," says Chernomyrdin. "It didn't happen."
